metadata.title: Hearing/vestibular problems, racial differences, and associations with physical function impairment among breast cancer survivors

sections.text: Abstract Background Breast cancer survivors face many health challenges, including tinnitus, hearing loss, and vertigo which will grow with an aging population and improved treatment outcomes. However, the prevalence of hearing/vestibular problems, racial differences, and relationships to physical function are poorly characterized in breast cancer survivors. Methods Between July and September 2023, we surveyed the Chicago Multiethnic Epidemiologic Breast Cancer Cohort. Tinnitus, hearing loss, and vertigo were self-reported and verified through electronic health records. Physical function impairment was measured using the SF-36 10-item instrument. We fit logistic regression models for hearing/vestibular problems and linear regression models for physical function score, controlling for sociodemographic and clinical factors. Results Of 1466 breast cancer survivors (mean [SD] age, 63.5 [11.8] years), 16.6%, 17.3%, and 8.6% reported experiencing tinnitus, hearing loss, and vertigo, respectively. Black survivors had lower odds of hearing loss (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] = 0.51; 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.31 to 0.86) but greater odds of vertigo (AOR = 2.29; 95% CI = 1.34 to 3.89) than White survivors. Survivors with hearing/vestibular problems had higher average impairment scores (worse physical function) than those without. In the adjusted regression models, survivors who reported experiencing tinnitus (β = 0.76; 95% CI = 0.10 to 1.43), hearing loss (β = 0.73; 95% CI = 0.06 to 1.40), or vertigo (β = 1.70; 95% CI = 0.81 to 2.58) had a higher level of physical function impairment. Conclusions This study demonstrates racial differences in hearing/vestibular problems and associations between these problems and physical function impairment. Survivorship programs should consider routine screening and interventions to improve hearing health and physical function among breast cancer survivors.

Breast cancer is the most common cancer and the second leading cause of cancer-related mortality among women in the United States, with Black women having a 40% higher mortality than White women. 1 , 2 With improved survival due to earlier diagnosis, treatment advances, and an aging population, the number of breast cancer survivors has increased and is expected to continue to rise. 3 , 4 As of January 1, 2025, there were approximately 4.3 million female breast cancer survivors in the United States, and 67.0% of them were aged ≥65 years. 5 Breast cancer diagnosis and treatment can have a detrimental impact on patients’ financial, physical, and psychosocial health and well-being. Black patients and survivors consistently experience worse breast cancer treatment outcomes and quality of life (QoL) than their White counterparts. 6-11 One potential consequence of cancer treatment is hearing/vestibular dysfunctions, including tinnitus, hearing loss, and vertigo. 12-14 Indeed, chemotherapy and radiotherapy are widely used to treat breast tumors, with neurosensory consequences. 15-18 Hearing/vestibular problems are prevalent among older adults and cancer survivors 19-24 and represent an emerging public health concern. A recent analysis of data from the 2011 to 2020 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey found that tinnitus (25.0% vs 17.0%) and troublesome hearing (41.0% vs 21.0%) were more prevalent in cancer survivors than in the general US population, and these differences remained statistically significant after adjusting for demographic and lifestyle factors, socioeconomic indicators, and comorbidities. 25 Research has reported a 30%–60% prevalence of tinnitus and a 34%-57% prevalence of hearing loss among adult cancer survivors of breast, gastrointestinal, gynecological, lung, oropharyngeal, or testicular cancer who underwent chemotherapy or radiotherapy. 26-30 Hearing/vestibular dysfunctions have been associated with worse QoL and shown to predict cognitive decline in US populations, including older adults, cancer patients, and cancer survivors. 19 , 24 , 28 , 31-36 Studies have also revealed that cancer survivors who experience tinnitus or hearing loss report clinically significant functional impairments 19 , 26 and lower physical function scores than those who do not experience these problems. 28 , 34 However, hearing/vestibular problems and physical function are poorly characterized among breast cancer survivors. 17-19 , 28 , 34 It is also unclear whether these problems vary across racial/ethnic groups in this aging population. Previous studies have been largely descriptive and have included cohorts of mixed cancer types and/or less diverse survivor populations. 23-30 , 34 To fill the knowledge gap, we sought to examine racial/ethnic differences in hearing/vestibular problems (Aim 1) and the associations between these problems and physical function impairment (Aim 2) among breast cancer survivors. To our knowledge, this study is the largest to evaluate hearing/vestibular problems and physical function in this growing survivor population.

This was a retrospective cohort study using survey and electronic health records (EHR) data. Between July and September 2023, we conducted a survey among participants in the Chicago Multiethnic Epidemiologic Breast Cancer Cohort (ChiMEC) to form a substudy cohort of breast cancer survivors. ChiMEC is an ongoing hospital-based cohort initiated in 2008, reaching more than 7000 patients with or without breast cancer. Since 2020, ChiMEC has been enhanced by annual surveys and patient contacts to improve the multidimensional data collection of survival, disease recurrence, QoL, and other health outcomes. Enrollment of new patients and follow-up of ChiMEC participants are ongoing. All participants provided written informed consent to the ChiMEC study and follow-up surveys. The University of Chicago Institutional Review Board reviewed and approved this study. We followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) reporting guidelines. 37

Figure S1 illustrates the cohort selection of breast cancer survivors. Briefly, we sent 3091 survey invitations to ChiMEC participants aged ≥18 years with available contact information via e-mail and postal mail. A total of 1492 patients responded to the survey, reflecting a 48.3% response rate. After excluding nonrespondents and those who did not complete their questionnaires, we obtained a final sample of 1466 breast cancer survivors.

The main outcomes for Aim 1 were hearing/vestibular problems including 3 conditions: tinnitus (ringing in the ears), hearing loss, and vertigo (persistent dizziness). In the survey, participants were asked whether they have ever been told by a doctor or other health-care providers that they have any of the conditions. Participants who reported hearing loss were also asked whether they used a hearing aid or had deafness in 1 or both ears not completely corrected by hearing aids. Through linkage to our patient EHR and local cancer registry, we verified self-reported conditions by checking the International Classification of Disease (ICD, versions 9 and 10) codes: tinnitus (ICD-9 codes: 388.30 to 388.32; ICD-10 codes: H93.11-H93.19); hearing loss (ICD-9 codes: 389.0, 389.14, 389.20 to 389.22, and 389.8 to 389.9; ICD-10 codes: H90.0 to 90.8, H91.0 to 91.9); and vertigo (ICD-9 codes: 386.10 to 386.11, 386.19, 386.2, and 438.85; ICD-10 codes: H81.1 to 81.4 and R42). We observed high specificity but low sensitivity when evaluating the concordance between self-reported and EHR-documented hearing/vestibular problems ( Table S1 ). Patients may not perceive these problems as severe and decide not to see a provider and therefore go undiagnosed clinically. On the other hand, patients may not recall prior episodes of these problems if they are no longer present. For Aim 2, the main exposures were hearing/vestibular problems as defined earlier. The main outcome was level of physical function impairment, which was measured using a 10-item instrument adopted from the 36-Item Short Form Health Survey Instrument. 38-40 The instrument assessed how the participants’ current health limited their ability to perform a range of activities during a typical day, including (1) vigorous activities, for example, running, lifting heavy objects, or participating in strenuous sports; (2) moderate activities, for example, moving a table, pushing a vacuum cleaner, bowling, or playing golf; (3) lifting or carrying groceries; (4) climbing several flights of stairs; (5) climbing 1 flight of stairs; (6) bending, kneeling, or stooping; (7) walking more than 1 mile; (8) walking several blocks; (9) walking 1 block; and (10) bathing or dressing yourself. For each activity, participants indicated the extent of limitation: not limited at all (score 0), limited a little (score 1), or limited a lot (score 2). The total score ranges from 0 to 20, with higher scores indicating greater levels of impairment (worse physical function). A 1-unit change in the physical function score is considered a minimally important difference, reflecting a clinically significant transition from no limitation to some limitation or from some limitation to a lot of limitation in at least 1 daily activity.

Participants reported their primary race and Hispanic ethnicity separately. Racial/ethnic groups included non-Hispanic Asian or Pacific Islander (hereafter, Asian or Pacific Islander), non-Hispanic Black (hereafter, Black), Hispanic, and non-Hispanic White (hereafter, White). It is important to note that race and ethnicity in this study were self-reported and therefore may not necessarily reflect biological differences. Additional sociodemographic characteristics included age at survey in years, marital status, highest level of education (high school or less, post–high school or some college, associate’s degree, bachelor’s degree, and graduate or professional degree), annual household income (<$50 000, $50 000–<$75 000, $75 000–<$100 000, $100 000–<$150 000, $150 000–<$200 000, and ≥$200 000), type of health insurance (Medicaid, Medicare, private, and other), smoking status, and alcohol consumption. Clinicopathologic factors included the Charlson-Deyo Comorbidity Index (CCI; 0, 1, and ≥2), American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) stage group, histologic type, receptor status, tumor grade, receipt of chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or hormone therapy, and type of surgery.

We first described the sample characteristics using summary statistics. Mean (SD) and median (interquartile range) were calculated for continuous variables, and frequency (%) were tabulated for categorical variables. Bivariate analyses, including t -tests, analysis of variance, Wilcoxon rank-sum, Kruskal-Wallis, Pearson’s χ 2 , and Fisher’s exact tests, were performed to compare survivors with hearing/vestibular problems to those without and across racial/ethnic groups. Restricted cubic spline logistic regression was used to estimate the rates of hearing/vestibular problems by age. This flexible approach allowed us to assess the shape of the relationships between continuous age and these problems. To examine racial/ethnic differences in hearing/vestibular problems, we fit 2 separate multivariable logistic regression models. Model 1 controlled for age at survey, AJCC staging, molecular subtype, tumor grade, and CCI. Model 2 further controlled for health insurance status, receipt of chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or hormone therapy, and type of surgery. Adjusted odds ratios (AORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated. To determine the associations between hearing/vestibular problems and physical function scores, we fit simple, age-adjusted, and 2 separate multiple linear regression models. On multivariable analyses, Model 1 controlled for age at survey, race/ethnicity, AJCC staging, and receipt of chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or hormone therapy. We included the race/ethnicity covariate in the model to adjust for the observed difference in the distribution of hearing/vestibular problems. Model 2 additionally controlled for CCI and type of health insurance. We calculated the variance inflation factor (VIF) for each variable in the regression models and did not detect the presence of multicollinearity ( Table S2 ). The residuals from the linear regression models are symmetrically distributed ( Figure S2 ) and our sample size is large. Thus, it is appropriate to rely on the Central Limit Theorem to use linear model. In our sensitivity analysis, we implemented a similar stepwise regression approach to assess the associations between EHR-confirmed hearing/vestibular problems and physical functioning. Adjusted linear regression coefficients (β) and 95% confidence intervals were computed. Hypothesis tests were 2-sided, with a significance threshold of P < .05. All data analyses were performed using Stata, version 18.0 (StataCorp LLC) from May 2024 to March 2025.

Of 1466 breast cancer survivors (mean [SD] age = 63.5 [11.8] years), 4.8% identified as Asian or Pacific Islander, 22.6% as Black, 3.0% as Hispanic, and 69.7% as White; and 41.1% had a graduate or professional degree ( Table S3 ). Most (71.7%) were privately insured, followed by 20.4% with Medicare and 4.6% with Medicaid. 6.4% and 7.0% had a CCI of 1 and ≥2, respectively. Moreover, 45.9% received chemotherapy and 66.5% received hormone therapy. The distributions of sociodemographic and clinical characteristics varied by race/ethnicity, where Black survivors were older, had lower levels of education and annual household income, were more likely to be on Medicaid or Medicare, and had more comorbidities ( Table S3 ).

sections.section: Racial And Age-Related Differences In Hearing/Vestibular Problems
sections.text: Overall, 16.6%, 17.3%, and 8.6% of breast cancer survivors reported having been told by a doctor or other health-care providers that they had tinnitus, hearing loss, and vertigo, respectively ( Table 1 ). The distributions varied between self-report and EHR, where higher proportions of tinnitus and hearing loss were captured by self-report and a higher percentage of vertigo was documented in EHR ( Figure S3 ). A higher proportion of Black survivors reported experiencing tinnitus (18.8%) than Asian or Pacific Islander (4.6%), Hispanic (10.0%), or White (17.1%) survivors ( P = .03) ( Figure 1 ). Black survivors also had a higher proportion of vertigo (13.6%), compared with Asian or Pacific Islander (1.6%), Hispanic (5.0%), or White (7.1%) survivors ( P < .001). The percentage of hearing loss was higher in White survivors (18.7%) than in Asian or Pacific Islander (12.1%), Black (12.9%), or Hispanic (12.2%) ( P = .06). The rates of tinnitus, hearing loss, and vertigo increased markedly with age. The rate of tinnitus increased from 5.0% at age 40 to 31.0% at age 90; hearing loss increased from 5.0% at age 40 to 50.0% at age 90; and vertigo increased from 5.0% at age 40 to 14.0% at age 90 ( Figure S4 ). After adjusting for demographic and clinical factors (Model 2), the odds of experiencing tinnitus were not significantly different between White and racial/ethnic minoritized survivors. Black survivors had lower odds of experiencing hearing loss than White survivors (AOR = 0.51; 95% CI = 0.31 to 0.86) ( Table 2 ). Asian or Pacific Islander and Hispanic survivors had no significant difference in hearing loss compared with White survivors. Black survivors had greater odds of experiencing vertigo (AOR = 2.29; 95% CI = 1.34 to 3.89) than White survivors ( Table 2 ). No significant differences in the odds of experiencing vertigo between Asian or Pacific Islander and White survivors and between Hispanic and White survivors. Older age was associated with greater odds of experiencing tinnitus (AOR = 1.63 per 10-year; 95% CI = 1.31 to 2.02) and hearing loss (AOR = 1.96 per 10-year; 95% CI = 1.56 to 2.47).

sections.section: Hearing/Vestibular Problems And Physical Function Impairment
sections.text: Overall, the distributions of physical function scores were significantly different between breast cancer survivors with hearing/vestibular problems and those without ( Figure 2 ). Specifically, survivors with tinnitus had a higher average score than those without (mean [SD] = 5.0 [5.1] vs 3.8 [5.0]; P = .001). The physical function impairment score was higher among survivors with vertigo than those without (mean [SD] = 6.3 [5.8] vs 3.8 [4.9]; P < .001). Compared with survivors with hearing loss, those without had a lower mean score (mean [SD] = 5.4 [5.5] vs 3.7 [4.9]; P < .001). Significant differences in physical function scores were also observed across EHR-documented vestibular problems ( Figure S5 and Table S4 ). In the unadjusted and age-adjusted linear regression models, hearing/vestibular problems were associated with higher levels of physical function impairment. Particularly, there was a dose-response relationship between hearing loss severity and physical function impairment ( Table S4 ). In multivariable analyses (Model 2), survivors with tinnitus (β = 0.76; 95% CI = 0.10 to 1.43), hearing loss (β = 0.73; 95% CI = 0.06 to 1.40), or vertigo (β = 1.70; 95% CI = 0.81 to 2.58) experienced higher levels of physical function impairment than those without ( Table 3 ). We observed similar patterns in the relationships between EHR-confirmed hearing/vestibular problems and physical function impairment ( Table S5 ).

This study found racial and age-related differences in hearing loss and vertigo and found that tinnitus, hearing loss, and vertigo were associated with physical function impairment among breast cancer survivors independent of demographic, health and cancer covariates. To our knowledge, this is the largest study to date that investigates hearing/vestibular problems and physical function in a large sample of breast cancer survivors. Given the growing and aging population of breast cancer survivors, survivorship programs should assess hearing/vestibular problems and functional impairments to inform intervention strategies and address unmet supportive care needs. In the ChiMEC cohort, 1 in 6 breast cancer survivors experienced tinnitus, more than 1 in 6 experienced hearing loss, and 9.0% experienced vertigo. The prevalence of hearing/vestibular problems varied by race/ethnicity. Particularly, Black survivors had a 49.0% lower likelihood of hearing loss than White survivors. This finding is aligned with results from epidemiologic studies of large US populations. 22 , 41-44 A study has shown that the odds of hearing loss were 32.0% lower in Black than in White older adults. 42 Research has examined imbalance and vertigo among cancer survivors but has not evaluated whether there were racial/ethnic differences. 17 , 18 , 23 , 24 , 31 , 32 Prior studies analyzing the US National Health Interview Survey and National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey data reported lower prevalence and odds of dizziness or vestibular vertigo in Black than White adults. 45 , 46 In contrast, Adams and Marmor found that Black adults had 8.0% higher odds of nonspecific dizziness than White adults, using a large administrative claims database (OptumLabs Data Warehouse). 47 Our study found that Black survivors were more than twice as likely as their White peers to experience vertigo. Taken together, these findings highlight racial differences in hearing/vestibular problems and suggest opportunities for screening and interventions to mitigate symptom disparities among breast cancer survivors. Age is a strong predictor of hearing/vestibular problems and functional status. Consistent with the findings among US older adults, 12 , 20 , 21 we observed increasing rates of hearing/vestibular problems as age increases and greater odds of physical function impairment among breast cancer survivors. This growing and aging survivor population bears a heavier symptom burden, needing tailored supportive care and social services. In 2014, the International Society of Geriatric Oncology updated its consensus on the recommendation of geriatric assessment (GA) among older cancer patients. 48 In 2023, the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) also published an updated guideline recommending GA and GA-guided care plan for older cancer patients and those who receive systemic therapy, covering domains across comorbidities, emotional health, nutrition, physical and cognitive function, polypharmacy, and social support. 49 Cancer centers should consider the implementation and integration of a comprehensive GA into their survivorship programs. These programs could conduct age-specific risk assessment, provide basic sensory function screening and gait and balance testing, and leverage EHR referrals to audiology, ENT, or vestibular physical therapy. Research is also necessary to evaluate GA in the breast oncology setting. Hearing and balance complaints and shared decision making should play an important role in these assessments, as survivors age and face these health challenges in the long term. Primary care, a central hub of care continuity after cancer treatment, can coordinate with oncology survivorship programs to create a comprehensive, personalized care plan for age-appropriate screenings, medication review, comorbidity optimization, and hearing aid access. Our study found relationships between hearing/vestibular problems and worse physical function among breast cancer survivors, where those with tinnitus, hearing loss, or vertigo experienced an increased level of physical function impairment. This finding is consistent with the existing literature in older adults and cancer patients and survivors. 19 , 24 , 28 , 30-34 , 36 , 50 For example, a secondary analysis of 750 cancer patients aged ≥65 years (with 22.0% being breast/gynecological cancers) reported that hearing and vision impairments were associated with reduced physical functioning. 19 Previous research has also suggested greater physical function impairment among cancer patients and survivors who have tinnitus, hearing difficulty or loss, and vertigo compared with those who do not. 24 , 28 , 31 , 34 In the breast cancer survivor population, older age, Black race, Hispanic ethnicity, late-stage diagnoses, receipt of hormone therapy, comorbidities, and public health insurance were additionally associated with lower levels of physical function. Our findings underscore the need for multifaceted interventions that address not only hearing/vestibular problems but also the clinical and socioeconomic disparities observed in physical function impairment. Social services, health navigation programs, and community health resources can help facilitate access to audiology, hearing aid, and vestibular therapy. Breast oncology programs can enhance multidisciplinary collaborations with audiology, physical therapy, geriatrics, and cancer survivorship. For example, programs can create GA-guided care plans for older patients with breast cancer per ASCO recommendations 49 and embed proper EHR prompts to ensure hand-offs and follow-through and improve team communications. In addition to GA implementation and integration aforementioned, survivorship programs should consider the practice of routine screening for hearing/vestibular problems and early interventions or treatment, such as audiology referrals, hearing aid use, and therapy for vertigo. Particularly, hearing aids can be beneficial to older breast cancer survivors with hearing loss. Recent studies have suggested that hearing aid use may slow short-term cognitive decline and reduce the risk of dementia among high-risk older adults. 51 , 52 Patient-provider discussion about hearing/vestibular problems and physical function are also encouraged, which can help identify individual needs and refer to appropriate supportive care and services. Moreover, research into the intersection of aging and multi-dimensional survivorship care in breast cancer is urgently needed. Evidence has shown that neurosensory and vestibular dysfunctions are associated with a higher level of social isolation, a lower level of social support, adverse mental health outcomes, comorbidities, and mortality across populations of older adults and cancer survivors. 19 , 23 , 26 , 31 , 36 , 50 The long-term impact of hearing/vestibular problems on the psychosocial well-being and mortality of breast cancer survivors has not been evaluated. Additionally, other neurosensory (eg, cognition, gustation/taste, olfaction/smell, and vision) dysfunctions in breast cancer survivors also remain understudied and are important directions for future research. This study has several limitations. First, self-reported data are often subject to recall error or social desirability bias. However, such bias is likely minimal in this study, as our research team had little to no direct interaction with respondents. In most cases, self-reported problems were verified and confirmed via patients’ EHR. Notably, our analysis of EHR-documented hearing/vestibular diseases yielded findings consistent with the self-reported data. Second, the sample included those who were willing to participate in the study, with a 48.3% response rate. Therefore, our prevalence estimates of tinnitus, hearing loss, and vertigo among breast cancer survivors may have been underestimated. Third, the low sensitivity regarding the concordance of hearing/vestibular problems between self-report and EHR indicates that these problems may not be well captured by patient self-report. This reflects that breast cancer survivors may forget previous episodes of hearing/vestibular problems if the problems are no longer present. It is also possible that these problems may not be severe enough to prompt them to seek care or follow-up with their providers. Misclassifications of hearing/vestibular problems were possible, but results based on self-reported and EHR data were consistent and similar. Fourth, unmeasured factors, such as noise and other environmental exposures, type of occupation, genetics, and behavioral factors, could potentially better explain the associations we observed in the study. Hence, future investigations should take account of these factors. Furthermore, we conducted multiple hypothesis tests and acknowledged that the study results were hypothesis generating. Last, ChiMEC cohort participants may not be representative of all breast cancer survivors and the general population in the United States, which may preclude the generalizability of our findings. However, we note that they may be generalizable to diverse, urban centers.

In this retrospective cohort study of racially diverse breast cancer survivors, hearing/vestibular problems varied by race/ethnicity, and experiencing these problems was associated with a higher level of physical function impairment. To improve breast cancer survivors’ hearing health and QoL, oncology survivorship programs should consider routine screening for hearing/vestibular problems, GA implementation and integration, and early interventions or treatment to identify and address unmet needs for supportive care resources.
